description: Dharma, the Purusharthas, sanatana dharma, varna, free will and the Hindu virtues (yamas).
content_html:
Dharma: Duty in Context

Dharma is one of the richest and most important concepts in Hinduism. The word has no single English equivalent: it can mean cosmic order, duty, righteousness, law, virtue or religion depending on context. For Hindus, dharma is the right way of living that upholds both individual moral integrity and the wider social and cosmic order. The Bhagavad Gita (II 31) teaches that it is better to carry out one’s own dharma imperfectly than to perform another’s dharma perfectly — emphasising that dharma is personal and contextual.

Sanatana dharma (‘eternal dharma’) is the name many Hindus prefer for their tradition, emphasising that its truths are not confined to a particular historical period or founder but are cosmic and universal. This framing presents Hinduism not as one religion among many but as the eternal truth about the nature of reality, the self and right action.

The Four Aims of Life: Purusharthas

Hindu teaching about human flourishing is organised around four legitimate aims of life, called the Purusharthas. These are:

  • Dharma — righteous conduct and duty. This aim frames all the others: the pursuit of wealth and pleasure must take place within the boundaries of ethical action.
  • Artha — material prosperity, security and success. The pursuit of artha is considered legitimate and necessary; Hindu teaching does not regard wealth as inherently bad, only as problematic if sought by unethical means or pursued to the exclusion of dharma and moksha.
  • Kama — pleasure, love and desire in their broadest sense. Again, this is a legitimate human aim; aesthetic pleasure, romantic love and physical enjoyment are not condemned but are to be pursued within dharmic boundaries.
  • Moksha — liberation from samsara. This is the highest aim, the one that gives ultimate meaning to all the others. The Bhagavad Gita (VIII 8–12) teaches that meditation and devotion to the divine leads ultimately to this final liberation.
Key Fact

The four Purusharthas are dharma (duty), artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure) and moksha (liberation). They present a holistic vision of human life: material and pleasurable aims are legitimate within the framework of dharma, with moksha as the ultimate horizon. This is different from traditions that treat wealth or pleasure as spiritually dangerous in themselves.

Varna, Ashrama and Social Dharma

Dharma is not the same for everyone: it varies according to a person’s varna (social class) and ashrama (stage of life). The combination of these two gives each person their specific dharmic duties. The Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) describes the qualities appropriate to each: Brahmins are to cultivate purity, wisdom and knowledge of the scriptures; Kshatriyas are to demonstrate courage, generosity and leadership; Vaishyas are to engage in trade and agriculture; Shudras are to serve the other varnas.

Contemporary Hindus hold divergent views on varna. Some interpret it as a flexible description of natural human temperaments and social functions, not a rigid hereditary system. Others (especially in reform movements influenced by thinkers such as Ambedkar) have challenged caste-based hierarchy as a distortion of dharma, arguing that the spirit of dharma requires equality of human dignity. This is a live debate within Hinduism.

Traditional interpretations hold that varna reflects the cosmic order established by Brahman and that each person’s role in society fulfils a purpose within that order. Reform movements argue that the hereditary caste system (jati), which evolved alongside varna, has been used to oppress Dalits (formerly ‘untouchables’) in ways that directly contradict dharma’s core commitment to righteous conduct. The Mahabharata (V 39) cautions that one should not do to others what one would not wish done to oneself — a golden rule principle that reformers apply to caste inequality.

Free Will, Suffering and Karma

A key question in Hindu thought is whether human beings are genuinely free. On one level, karma seems to determine future experience: the consequences of past actions are already in motion (parabdha karma). But Hinduism also affirms real free will — each person is always making choices (kriyamana karma) that shape the future. The Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) presents a list of divine qualities (such as fearlessness, purity and compassion) that a person can cultivate through conscious choice, suggesting that moral character is a genuine achievement, not simply the product of past karma.

Suffering is understood through karma: it is not a divine punishment or random cruelty, but the natural consequence of past actions working themselves out. This teaching can bring comfort (there is a reason) and challenge (it can be misused to blame those who suffer). Hindu traditions emphasise that recognising this law should inspire compassion for all sufferers, since all beings are working through their karma.

The Hindu Virtues: Yamas

Hindu ethical life is shaped by a set of moral duties known as yamas. These are ethical commitments that apply universally, regardless of a person’s social position. The Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) lists qualities that belong to those of a ‘divine nature’. The principal yamas include:

  • Ahimsa — non-violence or harmlessness. This is the most celebrated Hindu ethical principle, famously applied by Gandhi in his campaigns for independence. It requires not causing harm in thought, word or action to any living being. The Mahabharata (V 39) places ahimsa at the heart of dharma.
  • Daya — compassion. Recognising and responding with kindness to the suffering of others.
  • Dama — self-control and restraint. The Bhagavad Gita (VIII 8–12) presents disciplined meditation and self-mastery as essential to the path of liberation.
  • Dana — giving or generosity. Sharing resources freely is an expression of dharma and counters the ego-attachment that binds the atman to samsara.
Key Fact

Ahimsa (non-violence) is the foundational yama, described in the Mahabharata (V 39) as the highest dharma. The Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) lists compassion, self-control and generosity among the divine qualities. Together, the yamas describe a life that expresses dharma in every relationship.

Some commentators argue that the four Purusharthas are in tension: pursuing artha (wealth) and kama (pleasure) seems to pull in a different direction from moksha (liberation). Hindu thinkers respond that the framework is precisely designed to address this: dharma acts as the regulating principle, ensuring that the pursuit of wealth and pleasure does not become an end in itself. The gradual movement through the ashramas (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant) is understood as a natural progression from engagement with artha and kama towards deepening concern with dharma and finally moksha.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the Purusharthas, you must be able to name all four (dharma, artha, kama, moksha) and explain why dharma frames the others — this is a common exam point. When answering a 15-mark Discuss about Hindu ethics, use the yamas (especially ahimsa, supported by Mahabharata V 39) alongside the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) references. A very common error is treating the varna system as if all Hindus accept it uncritically — always note divergent views (reform vs traditional). Accurate spelling of ‘Purusharthas’, ‘sanatana dharma’, ‘ahimsa’, ‘yamas’ and ‘varna’ is rewarded in extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dharma is the right way of living according to one’s specific role and stage of life; sanatana dharma (‘eternal dharma’) is the name many Hindus give to their tradition as a whole, expressing its claim to timeless universal truth.
  • The four Purusharthas — dharma (duty), artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure) and moksha (liberation) — offer a holistic vision of human flourishing; dharma regulates the pursuit of artha and kama, with moksha as the ultimate goal.
  • The yamas (moral virtues) — especially ahimsa (non-violence), daya (compassion), dama (self-control) and dana (generosity) — are the ethical foundations of dharmic life; they are rooted in the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1–3) and the Mahabharata (V 39).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'sanatana dharma'.
practice_questions.marks: The eternal dharma; the name many Hindus use for their religion, indicating that its truths are ancient, universal and timeless. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Hindu virtue of ahimsa.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: ahimsa means non-violence or harmlessness; it requires not causing harm in thought, word or action to any living being; it is described as the highest dharma in the Mahabharata (V 39); Gandhi applied it in campaigns for independence; it is one of the central yamas (moral restraints). [2 marks — 1 for a simple statement, 2 for a developed description]

practice_questions.text: Outline the four Purusharthas (aims of human life) in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the four Purusharthas are dharma (duty/righteousness), artha (material prosperity), kama (pleasure/desire) and moksha (liberation); dharma acts as the regulating principle for artha and kama; moksha is the highest aim; together they present a holistic vision of human flourishing; the Bhagavad Gita (VIII 8-12) points towards moksha as the ultimate horizon. [3 marks — 1 for naming two or more Purusharthas, 2 for briefly describing them, 3 for a full outline explaining dharma's regulating role and moksha as the highest aim]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different Hindu views on the importance of varna (social division) in living according to dharma.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Traditional view: varna reflects the cosmic order established by Brahman; each social class has specific dharmic duties described in the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3); performing one's varna duty is a form of worship and keeps the social and cosmic order in harmony.
• Reform view: the hereditary caste system has been used to oppress Dalits, which contradicts the spirit of dharma as righteous conduct; the Mahabharata (V 39) golden rule ('do not do to others what you would not wish done to yourself') implies equality; thinkers such as Ambedkar challenged caste hierarchy as a corruption of genuine dharma.
[6 marks — 3 marks per view: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed explanation with a source or named position]

practice_questions.text: 'The concept of dharma is the most important Hindu teaching.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: dharma is described as the regulating principle that frames all other aims of life (Purusharthas); sanatana dharma is the name Hindus give to their entire religious tradition; the yamas (ahimsa, daya, dama, dana) all express dharma in practical terms; the Bhagavad Gita (II 31) teaches that one’s own dharma is irreplaceable; the Mahabharata (V 39) places ahimsa — an expression of dharma — at the centre of ethical life; without dharma, the pursuit of artha and kama becomes selfish and harmful.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: moksha (liberation) could be seen as more important because it is the ultimate goal that gives all other aims their meaning; the teaching on karma and samsara is arguably the foundation from which dharma draws its urgency; understanding Brahman (Saguna/Nirguna) is the deepest theological teaching; bhakti (loving devotion) traditions might argue that love of God is more central than duty; the concept of atman (the eternal self) is arguably prior to dharma since it explains why moral choices matter at all.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 31, XVI 1-3, VIII 8-12; Mahabharata V 39), explicit weighing of arguments, and a justified conclusion that takes a clear position.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching; conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed; some relevant content; limited source use.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and importance of the yamas in Hindu ethical life.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: yamas are moral restraints or virtues that apply to all human beings regardless of varna or ashrama; they include ahimsa (non-violence), daya (compassion), dama (self-control) and dana (generosity); the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3) describes qualities of a 'divine nature' that correspond to the yamas; they express dharma in everyday relationships; ahimsa is described as the highest dharma in the Mahabharata (V 39). [3 marks — 1 for identifying the yamas as moral virtues, 2 for explaining one or two with specific content, 3 for a full outline naming multiple yamas with their meaning and textual grounding]

glossary_terms.definition: Cosmic order, duty or righteous conduct; the right way of living that upholds the moral and cosmic order, varying according to a person's stage of life, social role and individual nature.
The eternal dharma; the name used by many Hindus for their religion, referring to the ancient, universal and timeless truths it embodies.
The four aims or goals of human life in Hinduism: dharma (duty/righteousness), artha (wealth/prosperity), kama (pleasure/desire) and moksha (liberation).
The four social divisions or classes in traditional Hindu society: Brahmin (priests and teachers), Kshatriya (warriors and rulers), Vaishya (traders and farmers) and Shudra (those who serve).
The four stages of life in Hindu tradition: brahmacharya (student), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (forest dweller) and sannyasa (renunciant).
Moral restraints or virtues in Hindu ethics; the foundational ethical commitments that apply to all human beings regardless of varna or ashrama.
Non-violence or harmlessness; the most fundamental Hindu ethical principle, requiring respect for all living beings.
Compassion; the quality of feeling and responding to the suffering of others.
Self-control or restraint; the discipline of mastering one's senses and impulses rather than being dominated by them.
Generosity or giving; the virtue of sharing one's resources and gifts with others, an expression of dharmic duty.
